﴿For every man among them is what he has earned of sin﴾ (24:11): each will be punished on the Day of Resurrection in accordance with his crime. What they earned is not good for them, because it is a crime for which they will be punished both in this worldly life and in the Hereafter.

(24:11) "Indeed, those who brought the slander are a group among you..." and "And he who took upon himself the greater part of it, for him is a great punishment" (24:11).

The one who took upon himself the greater part of this sin, who led this attack, kept this campaign going, and fanned its flames, was Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul. He was known, and still is known, by the title Ra'is al-Munafiqin (the chief of the hypocrites). He had raised the banners of this conspiracy. This man knew very well where to kindle the battlefield. Had Allah not encompassed all affairs, had He not taken upon Himself the protection of His religion and not arranged safeguards for His Messenger, this man would have made of things what he could.

It is narrated in the reports that when Safwan ibn Mu'attal brought the Mother of the Believers' camel-saddle and arrived at the camp, Ibn Salul was sitting among some people. He asked who this woman was, and the people said, "This is Aisha (رضي الله عنها)." He said, "By Allah, she could not have escaped from him, and he could not have escaped from her." Then he said, "Look, the wife of your Prophet spent the night with a man until morning, and now he is bringing her back."

He kept spreading these words day and night among his trusted people and continued his deep hypocritical schemes. His plots succeeded to such an extent that this baseless slander spread through Madinah like a forest fire, although all the circumstantial evidence was against it. Even some careless, devout Muslims began to speak, and for a full month this was the topic of conversation in Madinah, although the accusation was so flimsy that it could have been refuted the moment it was heard.

People even today cannot believe it and are astonished that such a base accusation could spread within Madinah, and then some careless individuals within the Muslim community began to discuss it. Thus those most exalted and pure personalities had to suffer such torment from this slander, especially the Master of both worlds (ﷺ).

This was a great psychological war. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fought this battle with great fortitude. The Muslim community fought this battle, and the whole of Islam fought this battle. I consider this to have been one of the most severe battles between Islam and disbelief, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims emerged from this battle victorious. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) kept hold of dignity and held fast to patient perseverance (sabr jamil), and proved that you (ﷺ) are a great man. Throughout this entire period, there is not a single report indicating that he showed impatience at any stage.

The pain, grief and sting that you (ﷺ) were feeling were such as you had never endured in your whole life. Yet you concealed everything. Islam had also never faced such a trial. Thus, because of this psychological war and propaganda war, the Muslim ummah was threatened.

Yet if anyone had reflected even a little in his heart, he could have reached the correct conclusion. If anyone had asked his heart for a verdict, the heart would have given him one. If anyone had adopted a natural approach, the reasoning of human nature would have become clear to him. The teaching of the Holy Qur'an was indeed this: that you should analyse circumstances, reflect deeply, and present your affairs before the judge of reason as well.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 24, verse 12:

(Lawla ... mubin) (24:12) "Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and believing women not think well of their own kind, and why did they not say, 'This is a clear calumny'?" Yes, it is true that the people of faith should have said this immediately upon hearing it. Had they dealt with their brothers in good opinion (husn al-zann), it would have been better for them. They should have supposed that a Muslim could not be involved in so vile an act. Furthermore, the pure wife of their Prophet and the companion concerned: they were of their own. Neither the sanctity (hareem) of the Prophet ﷺ nor that companion was fitting for such a matter as they had heard. They should have maintained good opinion, as Abu Ayyub Khalid ibn Zayd al-Ansari and his wife did.

Imam Ibn Ishaq has narrated: Abu Ayyub's wife, Umm Ayyub, said to him, "Do you not hear what people are saying about Aisha (ra)?" He said, "Yes, I hear it, but it is a lie. Umm Ayyub, would you do such a thing?" She said, "No, by God, I would never do it." He said, "Then Aisha is better than you."

Imam Mahmud ibn Umar al-Zamakhshari has related in his tafsir, al-Kashshaf, that Abu Ayyub said to Umm Ayyub, "Do you see what people are saying?" She said, "If you were in Safwan's place, could you have considered laying a hand on the honour of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?" He said, "Never." She said, "If I were in Aisha's place, I would not have betrayed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Aisha is better than me, and Safwan is better than you."

These two narrations show that some Muslims did reflect on this matter within themselves. They consulted their own hearts, and their intellects made them realise that it was not possible. And it is wrong to attribute this kind of baseness to any Muslim, and that too merely on the basis of suspicion and ill opinion.

This is the first path that the Qur'an indicates: that in any matter, after careful reflection and reasoning, one should form an opinion. Ask your own self, ask your own conscience. And elsewhere the Qur'an tells us that in any matter there must be evidence. Without proof and demonstration, no judgement should be made in such delicate matters.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 24, verse 13:

(Lawla ... humu al-kadhibun) (24:13) "This slander, which has enveloped very lofty personalities and laid hands on the honour of the purest of people, should not have been regarded as so easy and simple. Why was it circulated without proof, and why did it receive so much publicity? Why was it passed on from one person to another without any testimony? There was no evidence whatsoever in support of this accusation, so it should have been understood that a lie was being peddled. ﴿They are liars in the sight of Allah﴾. They are liars in accordance with the reality of the event, and the decision and command of Allah does not change. Therefore, this has become a permanent attribute of those who took part in the slander, and they can never escape its consequences.

These are the two methods. The first is to present any matter first before the mufti of reason and analogy, and to decide it within one's own heart and conscience. The second method is the law of evidence. In the incident of the slander (hadith al-ifk), ordinary people did not use either of these two methods, and everyone fell into the trap of the hypocrites. Then some believers also joined this campaign launched against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Yet this was a grave matter. Allah warns the believers so that they remain cautious in the future and do not repeat such an act."

(And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy in this world and the Hereafter, a great punishment would have touched you for what you plunged into.) (24:14)

Allah, the Exalted, caused this incident to occur as a trial for the newly formed community of Muslims, and then through His grace and mercy He resolved it in such a graceful manner. He did not punish anyone for this great error, though this act deserved severe punishment, because through this incident the people of Madinah had caused great distress to the Beloved of Allah (ﷺ). Therefore, it would have been appropriate for Allah to inflict severe punishment upon these people. Apart from the Prophet (ﷺ), in this incident his close companion, his beloved wife, and a truthful and pure Muslim were also made to suffer. Then, because of this great evil, all the sacred values of Islam were shaken to their foundations. The hypocrites had plotted this conspiracy so deeply that they wished to destroy the very foundations of the Islamic worldview. If the believers were to lose their trust in the Prophet, in the Prophet's family, and then in the Divine revelation, it is obvious that Islam would be considered finished. Such circumstances demanded that those who carried this fitnah be severely punished, and that Allah's punishment also descend upon them; but Allah, in His grace and generosity, ensured that the Muslims succeeded in this trial.

The state of affairs in Madinah throughout this entire month is well illustrated by the words of the Noble Qur'an, which show how great the intellectual confusion in Madinah was. How greatly the standards of the people had changed. How their values and criteria had been altered. What a mistake they were making at that time.

"When you were receiving it from one another with your tongues and saying with your mouths what you had no knowledge of, and you thought it a trivial matter while it was, in the sight of Allah, tremendous."

Without any reflection, without any thought or consideration, it was a matter that people kept repeating. It was as if this statement could not reach the heart and mind through the ears for contemplation, before another tongue snatched it up.

﴿And you used to say with your mouths that of which you had no knowledge﴾ (24:15). You were speaking with your mouths, yet you had no certain knowledge of it. Your hearts and minds were not prepared to accept it as a fact. These were words that merely flowed onto the tongues. These matters were not established by any knowledge or perception.

Then: ﴿And you thought it a trivial matter while it was, in the sight of Allah, tremendous﴾ (24:15). That is, you were levelling an accusation against the sanctity of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). You were causing pain to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his wife, a pain that was drying up his blood. Then you were levelling an accusation against the household of Hazrat Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (ra), against whom no accusation had been made even in the age of jahiliyyah. You were levelling this accusation against a companion of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who was a mujahid, while he was pure. Furthermore, through these accusations the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was being insulted. All these matters were so great in the sight of Allah that it was close to the point where the mountains would be moved, the sky would fall upon you, and you would be shaken to your core.

It would have been appropriate that, upon hearing this statement, the hearts of the Muslims should have recoiled from it. This statement should not have been voiced, and one should have refrained from making it a subject of discussion. The matter should have been left to Allah and His Messenger, and this false conspiracy should have been cast away from the pure Islamic atmosphere of Madinah like filth.

(Why did you not, when you heard it, say: "It is not for us to speak of this. Glory be to You! This is a tremendous slander"? (24:16))

When this matter is impressed upon the hearts of Muslims, the enormity of the lapse that people might fall into is made clear, and hearts are thoroughly shaken. People then understand how grave a fault they have committed, and they are warned: see that you never do such a thing again. You have committed a very great sin.

Allah admonishes you that you should never repeat the like of it, if you are believers (Qur'an 24:17).

"Allah admonishes you" (yaʿiẓukumu Allah): the admonition is delivered in an impactful, educative manner. This comes at a time when, after the mistake, people have come to realise how grave an error they committed, and when they are ready to listen, obey and trust. Even so, they are warned in strong words not to repeat this act. If you do so, your faith will be in danger, because believers accept admonition, and once it has been made clear to them how evil a deed they have done, it is now their duty, if they are believers, not to repeat it.

Allah makes the Verses clear to you, and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise. (24:18) As with the affair of the slander (ifk), He gave you guidance, laid bare the hidden aims behind it, and clarified the lapses that occurred among the Muslims themselves. And since Allah is All-Knowing, He also knows the intentions of all people. He knows the part each person played in this matter and the purpose they had in view, for He knows the secret depths of hearts. And the countermeasures Allah adopted in this matter are based on wisdom. Moreover, the laws He enacts are founded on profound wisdom, and they bring about the reform and welfare of people.

After this, a commentary on the incident of the slander (ifk) follows. In order to completely erase the effects and impressions that this incident left within society, and to purify the souls of the Muslims from it, the Muslims are once again warned that such an incident must not happen again. This time Allah showed grace and mercy, but in future, those who level such accusations against innocent, chaste women who are unaware of them will not escape the punishment of Allah, either in this world or in the Hereafter. This warning was issued so that, rising above worldly relationships and worldly currents, their ranks might be purified and illuminated anew. For example, the relationship between Hadrat Abu Bakr (رضي الله عنه) and his close relative Mistah ibn Uthathah was purified. This man too had become very active in that crisis in those days.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 24, verse 19:

(Inna alladhina... wa antum la ta'lamun) (24:19) "Those who love that indecency should spread among the believers deserve a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter. Allah knows, and you do not know."

Those who level accusations against chaste women, and especially those who dared to make baseless accusations against the Prophet's household (ḥarīm-i-Nabawī), their real desire is that they should shake the confidence in goodness, chastity and purity within the Muslim community, and spread such a false clamour about indecency that people become bold about it. People should say that this immorality is common even among great people. In this way, by spreading false stories, they heat up gatherings of indecency and make it widespread.

This is the effect of these false accusations. The Qur'an wants to make clear that indecency spreads because of false accusations, and therefore a painful punishment has been prescribed for such people in both this world and the Hereafter.

This is one of the methods of the Qur'an's style of moral training, and the purpose is to show that this law and punishment is one of the preventive measures, and that only Allah, who is the Creator of human psychology, can adopt these measures. He knows well how the human consciousness can be colored by these states and in what manner its direction can be given a good course. That is why Allah says:

Wa Allahu ya'lamu wa antum la ta'lamun (24:19): "Allah knows, and you do not know." Who knows human psychology better than the One who created it, and who can guide human conduct in a good manner other than the One who brought it into existence? Who is aware of the apparent and the hidden, and nothing is concealed from Him? He is indeed the All-Knowing, the All-Aware.

Allah once again draws the Muslims' attention to His grace and mercy.

(Wa lawla fadlullahi... raheem) (24:20) "And had it not been for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, and that Allah is Compassionate and Merciful..." Then this incident would have been a very grave one, and the mistake that you committed was no ordinary mistake. The mischief hidden within it would have caused you great harm. But it was the grace and mercy of Allah, and His kindness and His watchfulness, that He controlled the evil consequences of this great matter. Allah repeatedly mentions this point. Allah is making this incident a means of training, because its effects were falling upon the collective life of the Muslims.

Once it was made clear that this great calamity was close to shaking the collective system of the Islamic movement to its foundations, had it not been for the grace and mercy of Allah, now it is told: just think, you had set out upon the footsteps of Satan, who is your sworn enemy. "You should not follow in the footsteps of Satan. Henceforth, refrain from those satanic acts, as a result of which the whole society would be afflicted with such evil as a forest is engulfed by fire."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 24, verse 21:

(Ya ayyuha alladhina amanu... Wallahu Sami'un 'Alim) (24:21) "O you who have believed, do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Whoever follows Satan's footsteps, he will certainly command indecency and evil. Had it not been for the grace of Allah and His mercy upon you, not one of you would ever have been pure. But Allah purifies whom He wills, and Allah is Hearing and Knowing."

Would it be a pleasant sight if Satan keeps advancing and a believer keeps placing his foot in his footprints, when, of all human beings, the believer is most deserving of hating Satan and turning away from the path laid down by Satan to take the straight path? This is a repulsive image, which a believer abhors. His conscience and his awareness tremble at this scene. The mere thought of it makes his hair stand on end. This portrayal of following Satan startles a believer and makes him sensitive to avoiding the path of Satan.

(Wa man yattabi'... wal-munkar) (24:21) "Whoever follows Satan, he will command indecency and evil." The incident of the slander (al-ifk) is a very excellent example of this, as in it he implicated the whole population of Madinah. It is one of the repulsive deeds among Satan's achievements.

Man is very weak. He can fall prey to Satanic incitement and then also become involved in sin. Only the grace and mercy of Allah can protect him, but the grace and mercy of Allah will protect him only if he turns towards the grace and mercy of Allah and strives to walk on the method of Allah.

(Wa lawla fadlullah... yuzakki man yasha') (24:21) "Had it not been for the grace of Allah and His mercy upon you, not one of you would have ever been pure." This is because it is the light of the Lord that creates light in the heart and purifies and cleanses it. If there were not the grace of Allah and this light, not one of you would have remained pure and clean. Allah is Sami' and 'Alim. He purifies whom He wills, provided that there is goodness and capacity within him.

After this exhortation to purification and cleanliness, the believers are now advised that they should remove the bitterness that has arisen as a result of this evil, just as you hope for forgiveness from Allah, so too should you forgive one another.

(ولا یأتل۔۔۔۔۔۔۔۔ واللہ غفوررحیم) (24 : 22) "Let not those among you who are endowed with grace and ample means swear that they will not give to their kinsmen, the needy, and those who emigrated in the cause of Allah. They should pardon and overlook. Do you not wish that Allah should forgive you? And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful."

یہ آیت حضرت ابوبکر صدیق ؓ کے بارے میں نازل ہوئی ہے۔ اس وقت عائشہ صدیقہ ؓ کی برأت کا اعلان ہوچکا تھا۔ یہ بات ہمارے علم میں ہے کہ مسطح ابن اثاثہ ان لوگوں میں سے تھا جنہوں نے افک کے معاملے میں با تمہیں کیں۔ یہ حضرت ابوبکر صدیق ؓ کے قریبی رشتہ دار تھے اور فقرائے مہاجرین میں سے تھے ۔ حضرت ابوبکر صدیق ؓ ان پر خرچ کیا کرتے تھے۔ حضرت نے قسم اٹھا لی کہ وہ آئندہ مسطح کو کوئی فائدہ نہ دیں گے۔

Sayyid Qutb's commentary: This verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him). By then the innocence of Aisha al-Siddiqa (may Allah be pleased with her) had already been declared. It is known to us that Mistah ibn Uthathah was among those who spread slander in the affair of the ifk (the calumny). He was a close relative of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) and was among the poor Muhajirun. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) used to spend on him. He swore that he would no longer give Mistah any benefit.

یہ آیت نازل ہوئی۔ حضرت ابوبکر ؓ اور مومنین کو یاد دہانی کرائی گئی کہ وہ خود جب غلطیاں کرتے ہیں تو یہ امید رکھتے ہیں کہ اللہ انہیں معاف کردیں گے تو خود بھی ان میں بعض اگر بعض لوگوں کے بارے میں غلطی کریں تو ان کو معاف کرنا چاہیے۔ اور وہ جو بھلائی بھی کسی کے ساتھ کرتے تھے اسے نہ روکیں اگرچہ اس معاملے میں اس شخص سے غلطی ہوئی ہو۔

یہاں ہمیں پتہ چلتا ہے کہ یہ پاک دل لوگ کس قدر اونچی سطح کے لوگ تھے۔ ان کے دلوں کو نور ربانی نے پاک کردیا تھا۔ حضرت صدیق ؓ کا نفس کس قدر بلند اخلاقی کا نمونہ پیش کرتا ہے کہ اس واقعہ کے متاثرین میں سے وہ نہایت ہی گہرائی کے ساتھ متاثر ہوئے تھے۔ انہوں نے اس بہتان کی تلخیوں کو بہت ہی زیادہ جھیلا تھا۔ جب وہ اپنے رب کی نصیحت سنتے ہیں۔ جب یہ سوال ان کے پردہ وجدان کے ساتھ ٹکراتا ہے۔

(الآ تحبون ان یغفر اللہ لکم) (24 : 22) "Do you not wish that Allah should forgive you?" تو ان کی تمام رنجشیں ختم ہوجاتی ہیں۔ اب قبائلی اور خاندانی سوچ ختم ہوجاتی ہے یہاں تک کہ ان کی روح شفاف اور صاف ہوجاتی ہے۔ ان کے دل کی دنیا روشن ہوجاتی ہے۔ وہ پکار اٹھتے ہیں ہاں میں پسند کرتا ہوں کہ اللہ میرے گناہوں کو بخش دے۔ وہ مسطح کی امداد بحال کردیتے ہیں اور قسم اٹھاتے ہیں کہ جب تک وہ زندہ ہے اسے یہ امداد ملتی رہے گی۔ یہ فیصلہ اس قسم کے بدلے میں ہے کہ میں کبھی اسے کوئی نفع نہ پہنچائوں گا۔

یوں اللہ تعالیٰ اپنے رحم سے ان رنجیدہ دلوں کو جوڑتے ہیں اور اس معرکے کی وجہ سے ان کے اندر جو کدورتیں پیدا ہوگئی تھیں ان کو دھوڑالتے ہیں تاکہ یہ معاشرہ جس طرح پاک اور روشن تھا دوبارہ اسی طرح پاک اور روشن ہوجائے ۔

یہ مغفرت جس کا ذکر کیا گیا ان لوگوں کے لیے ہے جنہوں نے غلطی کی اور پھر توبہ کرلی اور آئندہ کے لیے وہ کسی پر الزام لگانے سے رک گئے۔ فحاشی کے پھلانے کا کام انہوں نے چھوڑ دیا۔ رہے وہ لوگ جو اپنی خباثت کی وجہ سے پاک دامن عورتوں پر الزام لگاتے ہیں۔ پھر اس پر اصرار کرتے ہیں مثلاً عبداللہ بن ابی ابن السلول اور اس جیسے دوسرے منافق تو ان کے ساتھ کوئی نرمی نہ ہوگی اور نہ انہیں معاف کیا جائے گا۔ اگر وہ اس دنیا میں قانون حد قذف سے بچ نکلے ۔۔۔ اس وجہ سے کہ ان کے خلاف اسلامی حکومت کے پاس گواہی نہیں ہے۔ آخرت کا عذاب تو ان کے انتظار میں ہے۔ وہاں تو گواہیوں کی ضرورت نہ ہوگی۔

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 24, verse 23:

(Inna alladhina yarmoona... huwa al-haqq al-mubin) (24:25) "Those who accuse chaste, unwary, believing women are cursed in this world and in the Hereafter, and for them is a great punishment. Let them not forget the day when their own tongues, hands and feet will bear witness against their deeds. On that day Allah will repay them in full what they deserve, and they will know that Allah is the Truth, the one who makes the truth manifest."

Here Allah presents the crime of these people in such a way that an unsuspecting woman, busy with some task of her own, is suddenly showered with arrows she never expected and against which she had no means of defence. In the same way, in the present case, a content and innocent woman was suddenly showered with arrows, while she had no expectation of anything of this kind. This is a crime of the sort that is extremely reprehensible, abominable and an oppressive assault. For this reason, the punishment of those who plan such a thing begins with the curse of Allah. The curse of Allah will be upon them, and in both this world and the Hereafter they will be deprived of the mercy of Allah. Then, on the Day of Resurrection, this will be their condition.

The Day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will bear witness against them concerning what they used to do. (24:24)

They will forget that day, though their own tongues, hands and feet will testify to their deeds. Some of them will then accuse others, saying: "You used to slander chaste, unsuspecting believing women!" This is a highly effective contrast within this scene: just as they used to level false accusations, so too will true accusations be leveled against them.

On that Day Allah will pay them their full recompense, their due (24:25). "On that Day Allah will pay them their full recompense, their due." On that day Allah will also disgrace them, and this will be a fitting punishment, because they disgraced innocent people. Their account will be given to them in full, and on that day they will come to believe in the things they were not believing in.

"And they will know that Allah is the Truth, the Manifest" (24:25). "And they will know that Allah is the Truth, the one who makes the truth manifest." The discourse on the incident of the slander (ifk) concludes with this point: the practical outcome of the freedom Allah has given to human beings, which is present in people's practical lives, is that a corrupt soul is joined to a corrupt soul, and a good and pure soul is joined to a pure soul. According to this principle, it is only possible that the union of Hadrat Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her) is with the purest soul. Therefore, the accusation of these people is also false in this respect, that in the division of destiny, Aishah the Truthful (may Allah be pleased with her) fell to the share of Hadrat Muhammad (ﷺ), and so she is pure (tayyibah).

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 24, verse 26:

(Al-khabithat... wa rizqun karim) (24:26) "Evil women are for evil men, and evil men for evil women. Good women are for good men, and good men for good women. They are free from what the slanderers say; for them is forgiveness and an honourable provision."

Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) had immense love for Hazrat Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her). How could Allah have chosen her for His Prophet if she were not pure? These pure people, by their very nature, are free from those things, and they are far removed from the vile accusations that are attributed to them.

For them there is an honourable provision in the Hereafter, and forgiveness for their sins, meaning that their minor shortcomings are pardoned by Allah.

With these verses, the events of the slander (al-ifk) come to a conclusion. Because of these events, the Muslim community had fallen into great distress. As a result of that incident, the purity and honour of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his household was a matter of serious concern. Alongside the trials of great battles, this was also a trial from Allah, meant to strengthen the internal front, through which the early Islamic community was made to pass.

Lesson No. 153: At a Glance

As we have said before, in building a pure society Islam does not rely solely on severe punishments. Islam first adopts preventive and deterrent measures against crime. Moreover, Islam neither suppresses nor destroys man's natural desires; rather, it provides a most pure and normal environment for those natural desires, one free of any artificial provocation.

In this context, the basic principle of Islam's system of moral training is blocking the means. Islam closes the very doors that lead to straying, eliminates the causes that become means of leading man astray, or provide the causes of temptation, or through which emotions of man are inflamed. On the other hand, Islam also provides people with the means of natural gratification, within the bounds of the law.

Islam deeply respects the family and the sanctity of the home. Therefore, the first principle established is that no one may enter someone's home without the permission of its inhabitants. This is solely so that the eyes of the one entering do not see any scene that the household wishes to keep hidden. Now, if someone enters suddenly and the household is unprepared, they would not like that sight. Furthermore, Islam also commands that all men and women lower their gaze, and that women do not go out adorned with beautification.

Along with this, Islam provides opportunities for the poor and the needy to marry, because the best weapon against immorality is to bring all people within the secure fortress of marriage. Likewise, it is commanded that slave girls should not be compelled to immorality, since immorality can very easily be spread through slave girls.

Lesson No. 153: Explanation of the Verses
27 to 34

(O you who believe, do not enter... until you have sought permission...) (24:27–29)

Allah made homes a place of tranquility for mankind. People return to them after working, and their souls find peace there, and their selves find rest there. Here they are at ease regarding their private and hidden affairs, their honour is safe here, and here they rest and soothe their nerves.

Such rest and tranquility in a home can be achieved only when no outsider lays a hand on the sanctity of the four walls, and the household lives in complete peace and security, except when someone enters from outside with their permission. And he should enter at the time they wish, and in circumstances in which the household grants permission.

Now, if someone is given permission to enter another's home, and his eyes see a scene that becomes a temptation for both, and the sudden entry becomes the cause of that temptation for him, then in this way the possibility of immorality spreading in society arises. Sometimes the repetition of such glances becomes a trial. Although the first meeting is sometimes without intention or purpose, later it becomes a temptation. When both parties take one step further, the result is corruption, immorality and deviation.

In the days of jahiliyyah, people would suddenly enter one another's homes. The visitor would arrive first and then say, "I have come." Sometimes the master of the house would be with his family in a state in which entering from outside would be objectionable, yet they would not care. Sometimes a woman in the house would be naked, or her private parts would be exposed, or a man would be in such a state. This would cause distress to the master of the house and destroy the peace and tranquility of another's home. Whereas sometimes such an unexpected incident became the cause of temptation, as the eye would see a scene from which a trial would arise.

Keeping all these matters in view, the Qur'an made Muslims bound by these etiquettes: that entering someone's home without permission is forbidden. It is proper that greetings of peace be given from outside, so that they come to know that such-and-such a person wishes to come in. Moreover, through this manner a kind of familiarity is also created.

(O you who believe, do not enter houses other than your own until you have asked permission and greeted their inhabitants) (24:27). Here the expression for seeking permission is expressed by the word "anas" (to seek familiarity). This manner of expression points to the most refined way of seeking permission. It also indicates that the one arriving should come in a most courteous manner, speaking with people with great warmth and courtesy, so that they may be prepared to receive him. This is an extremely subtle and profound moral principle, for the people's convenience, for restoring their dignity and honour in their homes, and so that the household does not become weary, day and night, of visitors, one coming and another going, and that too without permission.

As a result of permission, the situation will be this: either someone will be in the house and will grant permission, in which case this person may enter the house; and if no one is there, then this person is not permitted to enter.

(And if you find no one therein, do not enter until permission is given to you) (24:28). If someone from the household is present inside, merely asking for permission does not grant entry unless they explicitly give permission. If those inside do not permit, one should return without any hesitation, and should not wait.

(And if you are told, "Go back," then go back; it is purer for you) (24:28). That is, return without any bitterness, without the impression that the household has wronged you or harbours any hatred toward you, because the household has its own secrets and excuses. Therefore it is necessary to grant them the right to decide whether at that time they can receive a guest or not.

(And Allah is Knowing of what you do) (24:28). Allah is the One who knows the hidden secrets of hearts, or that He is aware of the emotions and thoughts within hearts.

As for places that are public, such as hotels, inns, guesthouses, hostels and the like, which are separate from private residences, entering them without permission is permissible when there is no cause requiring permission.

(There is no blame upon you for entering houses not inhabited, in which there is [some] benefit for you) (24:29). 

(And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal) (24:29). The fundamental point is that Allah knows your outward and inward states, and He is your Overseer. He is aware of your inner thoughts, of what your inner intentions are. Therefore, Allah prescribes for you, in His Book, a most courteous way of life. He is also your Overseer, and His demand is that you obey Him sincerely in the heart.

The truth is that the Qur'an is a complete system of life, and therefore it treats even a very minor matter of human life in such detail, because the subject of this system is the conduct of human life, whether minor or detailed. In this way Islam establishes a balance between the fundamentals and the branches of the system. The law of seeking permission is one measure to make homes places of peace and security. The purpose of this measure is that no resident of a home should suddenly be confronted with an undesirable situation, because when someone enters suddenly, one does not know in what condition the people inside are. It may be that someone's head is uncovered, or that someone's private parts are exposed. The word "awrat" (nakedness/private matters) carries a broader meaning; it does not refer only to bodily nakedness. It also includes arrangements for food and drink, clothing, furnishings, places of sitting and rising, and household goods, which the household does not want anyone to enter upon without preparation, and to find the inner condition in a state of lesser psychological ease. For example, few would like someone to enter while someone inside is weeping, or while the master of the house is angry, or while he is afflicted with some pain and sorrow that he wishes to keep hidden from the public. All of these are awrat.

Through this single "etiquette," the Qur'an gathers countless benefits. Some we know, and some we do not know. Moreover, the important point is that a person can also be protected from sudden glances, which give rise to the emergence of forbidden desires, and afterwards these relationships take the form of evil relationships. In short, the etiquette of the Qur'an is a most beneficial and important means of reform for controlling the straying of glances and the sudden attraction of hearts.

Only those people understand its reality and importance in whom this etiquette first descended, and it was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who initiated it through his own practice.

Imam Abu Dawud and Nasa'i narrated the hadith of Abu Amr al-Awza'i, who related from Qays ibn Sa'd that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to our dwelling and said from outside, "As-salamu alaykum." Sa'd replied gently, "Wa alaykum as-salam," but softly. Qays says: I said to Sa'd, "Do you not want to let the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in?" He said, "Leave it, let him greet us a bit more." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said a second time, "As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah," and Sa'd again answered quietly, "Wa alaykum as-salam." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah," and then he returned. Sa'd came out of the house and called out, "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)!" I was hearing you and answering your salutation quietly, desiring that you would greet us abundantly. The narrator says the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned with him. Sa'd ordered that water be prepared for the bath of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He bathed. Then Sa'd presented to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) a flowered woollen cloth, which was dyed with saffron or with the herb "dars." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrapped himself in it. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) raised his hands and made this supplication:

"Allahumma aj'al salatika wa rahmatika ala ali Sa'd ibn Ubadah." "O Allah, place Your blessings and mercy upon the family of Sa'd ibn Ubadah."

Abu Dawud narrated the hadith of Abdullah ibn Bishr. He says: when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to the door of a people, he would not stand facing the door directly, nor to its right or left side, but would say, "As-salamu alaykum... As-salamu alaykum." At that time, homes did not have curtains.

Abu Dawud narrated from Hudhayl that a man came (Uthman says it was Sa'd) and stood at the door of the Prophet (ﷺ) and began seeking permission to enter. He stood facing the door directly. (Uthman said: facing the door.) The Prophet (ﷺ) then taught him the method and said, "Stand like this, for seeking permission has been enjoined so that you do not see inside."

In the Sahihayn it is recorded that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: if someone enters your house without permission, and you throw a pebble at him and it blinds his eye, you will bear no blame.

Abu Dawud narrated from Rab'i that a man from the Banu Amir sought permission to enter upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was in his house. He said, "Shall I come in?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said to his servant, "Go out and teach this man the method of seeking permission to enter. Tell him to say, 'As-salamu alaykum, may I enter?'" The man heard the Prophet's words and said, "As-salamu alaykum, may I enter?" The Prophet (ﷺ) gave him permission, and he entered.

Haytham said that Mughirah said, and Mughirah said that Mujahid said: Umar came on a certain need, and the heat troubled him. He came to the tents of a woman of Quraysh and said, "As-salamu alaykum, may I come in?" She said, "Enter in peace." Umar sought permission again, and she gave the same reply, although he was standing at her feet. Then Umar said, "Say 'udkhul' (enter)." Upon this, the woman said, "Enter." Then he entered.

Ata ibn Abi Rabah narrated from Ibn Abbas. He said: I asked, "Should I seek permission even from my orphaned sisters who are in my own house under my care?" He said, "Yes." I then questioned him again so that I might be given leave. He said, "Would you like to see her naked?" I said, "No." He said, "Then seek permission." I argued with him again, and he said, "Do you want to obey the command of Allah or not?" I said, "Yes." "Then seek permission," he said.

And in a sound hadith it comes that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: no one should suddenly return to his household at night. In some narrations it comes: "lay yatakhawwanahum" (lest he betray them). And in another hadith it comes that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived at Madinah during the day, and before the city he made his camels kneel. He said, "Wait until the evening, that is, until the last part of the day, so that a woman whose hair is disheveled may comb it, and a woman whose hair is unkempt may tidy it."

Islam taught Muslims the most courteous manners and had the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) put them into practice. These lofty etiquettes were given to those who were most radiant and illuminated by the divine light.

Today we too are Muslims, but our sense of such matters has become coarse. We have become boorish. A person goes to his brother's house and darts inside like an arrow, entering at whatever hour of the day or night he pleases. He rings the bell again and again, and only stops when someone gets up reluctantly and opens the doors for him. Sometimes there is a telephone in the house. He could ask permission very conveniently and fix a time. But we have abandoned Islam's system of seeking permission (istidhan), and we arrive at other people's homes at any time without warning. Now we have come to regard leaving without a meeting as improper, even when the household does not wish it. Our attitude is that once we have arrived, we are bound to walk in, without any hesitation or waiting.

We are Muslims, yet we disturb our brothers when they sit down to eat. If they do not offer us food, we take offence. We go to visit late into the night. If they do not invite us to stay the night, we take offence, and we are not ready to hear anyone's excuse in such matters. This happens simply because we are not steeped in Islamic etiquette. We do not want to bring our desires under the discipline that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought. In truth, we have become slaves to a wrong, pre-Islamic custom for which Allah has provided no proof.

What is even stranger is that we see people who have not accepted Islam practising certain etiquettes that resemble our religion. These are precisely the etiquettes that our religion taught us. We are astonished to see these non-Muslims observing the etiquettes of our religion, while we ourselves do not know our own religion. Instead, we are impressed by them and regard these as rare manners. Even having reached this stage, we make no effort to understand our religion, and we remain content that we are Muslims.

After the etiquette of entering homes, through which precautionary and preventive measures have been adopted so that no one falls into the trial of the gaze and its harmful consequences, believers are now given a general exhortation to guard their gaze, for gazing lustfully is what leads a person to misguidance and waywardness.

﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do. And say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts, and not display their adornment except what necessarily appears of it, and that they should draw their head-coverings over their chests, and not display their adornment except to their husbands, their fathers, their husbands' fathers, their sons, their husbands' sons, their brothers, their brothers' sons, their sisters' sons, their women, those whom their right hands possess, male attendants who have no physical desire, or children who are not yet aware of women's private matters. And they should not stamp their feet so as to reveal what they conceal of their adornment. O believers, turn to Allah in repentance, all of you, that perhaps you may prosper.﴾ (30:31)

The aim of these verses is to establish a very pure and clean society, one in which there is not constant sexual agitation everywhere and at all times, and in which there are not constant means of enjoying flesh and bone. Measures that continually stir up sexual excitement, and as a result produce a thirst that is never quenched, are harmful. A malicious glance, a seductive gesture, the display of adornment, and the exposure of the body can set the feelings of others on fire. They do not merely awaken the dormant animality within a person, but also create restlessness in the other party. The other side then loses control over itself. Either the person falls prey to unrestrained sexual indulgence, or nervous and psychological disorders arise within him, and in this way a person is afflicted with suffering.

Islam, which seeks to build a pure and clean society, adopts as its first measure for establishing it the protection of feelings from agitation. It preserves the natural inclinations found in both parties, and gives this natural impulse a protected and constructive form in accordance with its natural pattern.

There came a period in human history when the doctrine of ibahiyyah (permissiveness) spread. Free conversation between the sexes, free mixing, and idle chatter were made common, to the extent that children began to be given sexual education, and the most secret matters were brought into the open. These things and measures were undertaken under the doctrine that they protect people from the harms of suppressing sexual inclination and sexual feelings, and that they give people the opportunity to make sexual arrangements freely as they wish. These doctrines permitted this so that people would not commit violence and other wrongdoing in the sexual sphere.

This sexual freedom became prevalent when purely materialist views about human beings spread, and the human being was declared to be merely an animal, especially after the spread of Freud's sexual ideas. But I myself observed these doctrines in a country where there was complete permissiveness, and where none of the religious, moral or human restraints existed. Yet I observed that all these doctrines are mere assumptions, and that the conditions of such countries utterly refute them.

We have also seen countries in which there is no restriction on physical union, nudity, and sexual licentiousness. There, all its possible forms are lawful. But in those countries sexual relations did not become civilised, nor did any regularity arise within them. Rather, sexual thirst grew to the point of madness, and grew so much that the very trace of satisfaction disappeared. In those countries a flood of sexual and psychological diseases broke out, and problems emerged that arise from sexual deprivation. These problems are found abundantly in those societies in which there is no restriction on sexual anarchy. These problems arose simply because in such countries there was no sexual restraint or discipline. Sexual friendships were free without any obstacle, and sexual relations and unions were seen on the roads like those of cattle. Sexual movements and lustful glances were quite ordinary things. The detailed events and detailed conduct of these countries cannot be discussed here. For details, see Muhammad Qutb's book (Al-Insan bayna al-Maddiyyah wal-Islam), the chapter on sexual problems. For further details, see my forthcoming book (Amrika allati Ra'ayt) (America as I Saw It).

Attraction between men and women is a natural matter, and it has been innately placed within human beings, because the continuity of life on this earth depends upon it. Human beings have the responsibility of discharging the duties of vicegerency (khilafah) on the earth. A large and important part of this responsibility is to maintain the continuity of life here. Therefore this attraction is a permanent attraction. Sometimes it falls asleep and then awakens again. As soon as it awakens, it is fulfilled only when union between the two sexes takes place and satisfaction is achieved. If this physical satisfaction does not occur, its effect falls upon the human nerves, and in such circumstances a person feels intense oppression. Then even a glance can incite him, a gesture can incite him, and even a slight smile can arouse him. As a result of mere idle chatter, a person becomes uncontrollable, and even a beautiful voice can set him trembling. Therefore the safe course is to protect a person within society from such occasions, so that his sexual inclination remains within natural limits, and so that opportunities for his satisfaction are provided through lawful and natural means. Islam adopts precisely this method. Alongside this, Islam also turns a person's powers towards other constructive directions. The other affairs of life are of greater importance than the mere union of body, soul, flesh and bone, so sexual gratification does not remain the only goal before a person. The verses under discussion put into operation exactly such policies of Islam, namely: reducing the occasions that produce agitation, engaging people in lofty objectives, and then creating opportunities for lawful satisfaction for both parties.

When both parties take one step further, the result is corruption, immorality and deviation.

In the days of jahiliyyah, people would suddenly enter one another's homes. The visitor would arrive first and then say, "I have come." Sometimes the master of the house would be with his family in a state in which entering from outside would be objectionable, yet they would not care. Sometimes a woman in the house would be naked, or her private parts would be exposed, or a man would be in such a state. This would cause distress to the master of the house and destroy the peace and tranquility of another's home. Whereas sometimes such an unexpected incident became the cause of temptation, as the eye would see a scene from which a trial would arise.

Keeping all these matters in view, the Qur'an made Muslims bound by these etiquettes: that entering someone's home without permission is forbidden. It is proper that greetings of peace be given from outside, so that they come to know that such-and-such a person wishes to come in. Moreover, through this manner a kind of familiarity is also created.

(O you who believe, do not enter houses other than your own until you have asked permission and greeted their inhabitants) (24:27). Here the expression for seeking permission is expressed by the word "anas" (to seek familiarity). This manner of expression points to the most refined way of seeking permission. It also indicates that the one arriving should come in a most courteous manner, speaking with people with great warmth and courtesy, so that they may be prepared to receive him. This is an extremely subtle and profound moral principle, for the people's convenience, for restoring their dignity and honour in their homes, and so that the household does not become weary, day and night, of visitors, one coming and another going, and that too without permission.

As a result of permission, the situation will be this: either someone will be in the house and will grant permission, in which case this person may enter the house; and if no one is there, then this person is not permitted to enter.

(And if you find no one therein, do not enter until permission is given to you) (24:28). If someone from the household is present inside, merely asking for permission does not grant entry unless they explicitly give permission. If those inside do not permit, one should return without any hesitation, and should not wait.

(And if you are told, "Go back," then go back; it is purer for you) (24:28). That is, return without any bitterness, without the impression that the household has wronged you or harbours any hatred toward you, because the household has its own secrets and excuses. Therefore it is necessary to grant them the right to decide whether at that time they can receive a guest or not.

(And Allah is Knowing of what you do) (24:28). Allah is the One who knows the hidden secrets of hearts, or that He is aware of the emotions and thoughts within hearts.

As for places that are public, such as hotels, inns, guesthouses, hostels and the like, which are separate from private residences, entering them without permission is permissible when there is no cause requiring permission.

(There is no blame upon you for entering houses not inhabited, in which there is [some] benefit for you) (24:29). 

(And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal) (24:29). The fundamental point is that Allah knows your outward and inward states, and He is your Overseer. He is aware of your inner thoughts, of what your inner intentions are. Therefore, Allah prescribes for you, in His Book, a most courteous way of life. He is also your Overseer, and His demand is that you obey Him sincerely in the heart.

The truth is that the Qur'an is a complete system of life, and therefore it treats even a very minor matter of human life in such detail, because the subject of this system is the conduct of human life, whether minor or detailed. In this way Islam establishes a balance between the fundamentals and the branches of the system. The law of seeking permission is one measure to make homes places of peace and security. The purpose of this measure is that no resident of a home should suddenly be confronted with an undesirable situation, because when someone enters suddenly, one does not know in what condition the people inside are. Through this single "etiquette," the Qur'an gathers countless benefits. Some we know, and some we do not know. Moreover, the important point is that a person can also be protected from sudden glances, which give rise to the emergence of forbidden desires, and afterwards these relationships take the form of evil relationships. In short, the etiquette of the Qur'an is a most beneficial and important means of reform for controlling the straying of glances and the sudden attraction of hearts.

Islam taught Muslims the most courteous manners and had the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) put them into practice. These lofty etiquettes were given to those who were most radiant and illuminated by the divine light.

A person goes to his brother's house and darts inside like an arrow, entering at whatever hour of the day or night he pleases. He could ask permission very conveniently and fix a time. But we have abandoned Islam's system of seeking permission (istidhan), and we arrive at other people's homes at any time without warning. Now we have come to regard leaving without a meeting as improper, even when the household does not wish it. Our attitude is that once we have arrived, we are bound to walk in, without any hesitation or waiting.

We are Muslims, yet we disturb our brothers when they sit down to eat. If they do not offer us food, we take offence. We go to visit late into the night. If they do not invite us to stay the night, we take offence, and we are not ready to hear anyone's excuse in such matters. This happens simply because we are not steeped in Islamic etiquette. We do not want to bring our desires under the discipline that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought. In truth, we have become slaves to a wrong, pre-Islamic custom for which Allah has provided no proof.

﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do. And say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts, and not display their adornment except what necessarily appears of it, and that they should draw their head-coverings over their chests, and not display their adornment except to their husbands, their fathers, their husbands' fathers, their sons, their husbands' sons, their brothers, their brothers' sons, their sisters' sons, their women, those whom their right hands possess, male attendants who have no physical desire, or children who are not yet aware of women's private matters. And they should not stamp their feet so as to reveal what they conceal of their adornment. O believers, turn to Allah in repentance, all of you, that perhaps you may prosper.﴾ (30:31)

The aim of these verses is to establish a very pure and clean society, one in which there is not constant sexual agitation everywhere and at all times, and in which there are not constant means of enjoying flesh and bone. Measures that continually stir up sexual excitement, and as a result produce a thirst that is never quenched, are harmful. A malicious glance, a seductive gesture, the display of adornment, and the exposure of the body can set the feelings of others on fire. They do not merely awaken the dormant animality within a person, but also create restlessness in the other party. The other side then loses control over itself. Either the person falls prey to unrestrained sexual indulgence, or nervous and psychological disorders arise within him, and in this way a person is afflicted with suffering.

Islam, which seeks to build a pure and clean society, adopts as its first measure for establishing it the protection of feelings from agitation. It preserves the natural inclinations found in both parties, and gives this natural impulse a protected and constructive form in accordance with its natural pattern.

There came a period in human history when the doctrine of ibahiyyah (permissiveness) spread. Free conversation between the sexes, free mixing, and idle chatter were made common, to the extent that children began to be given sexual education, and the most secret matters were brought into the open. These things and measures were undertaken under the doctrine that they protect people from the harms of suppressing sexual inclination and sexual feelings, and that they give people the opportunity to make sexual arrangements freely as they wish. These doctrines permitted this so that people would not commit violence and other wrongdoing in the sexual sphere.

This sexual freedom became prevalent when purely materialist views about human beings spread, and the human being was declared to be merely an animal, especially after the spread of Freud's sexual ideas. But I myself observed these doctrines in a country where there was complete permissiveness, and where none of the religious, moral or human restraints existed. Yet I observed that all these doctrines are mere assumptions, and that the conditions of such countries utterly refute them.

We have also seen countries in which there is no restriction on physical union, nudity, and sexual licentiousness. There, all its possible forms are lawful. But in those countries sexual relations did not become civilised, nor did any regularity arise within them. Rather, sexual thirst grew to the point of madness, and grew so much that the very trace of satisfaction disappeared. In those countries a flood of sexual and psychological diseases broke out, and problems emerged that arise from sexual deprivation. These problems are found abundantly in those societies in which there is no restriction on sexual anarchy. These problems arose simply because in such countries there was no sexual restraint or discipline. Sexual friendships were free without any obstacle, and sexual relations and unions were seen on the roads like those of cattle. Sexual movements and lustful glances were quite ordinary things. The detailed events and detailed conduct of these countries cannot be discussed here. For details, see Muhammad Qutb's book (Al-Insan bayna al-Maddiyyah wal-Islam), the chapter on sexual problems. For further details, see my forthcoming book (Amrika allati Ra'ayt) (America as I Saw It).

Attraction between men and women is a natural matter, and it has been innately placed within human beings, because the continuity of life on this earth depends upon it. Human beings have the responsibility of discharging the duties of vicegerency (khilafah) on the earth. A large and important part of this responsibility is to maintain the continuity of life here. Therefore this attraction is a permanent attraction. Sometimes it falls asleep and then awakens again. As soon as it awakens, it is fulfilled only when union between the two sexes takes place and satisfaction is achieved. If this physical satisfaction does not occur, its effect falls upon the human nerves, and in such circumstances a person feels intense oppression. Then even a glance can incite him, a gesture can incite him, and even a slight smile can arouse him. As a result of mere idle chatter, a person becomes uncontrollable, and even a beautiful voice can set him trembling. Therefore the safe course is to protect a person within society from such occasions, so that his sexual inclination remains within natural limits, and so that opportunities for his satisfaction are provided through lawful and natural means. Islam adopts precisely this method. Alongside this, Islam also turns a person's powers towards other constructive directions. The other affairs of life are of greater importance than the mere union of body, soul, flesh and bone, so sexual gratification does not remain the only goal before a person. The verses under discussion put into operation exactly such policies of Islam, namely: reducing the occasions that produce agitation, engaging people in lofty objectives, and then creating opportunities for lawful satisfaction for both parties.

Lesson No. 153: At a Glance

As we have said before, in building a pure society Islam does not rely solely on severe punishments. Islam first adopts preventive and deterrent measures against crime. Moreover, Islam neither suppresses nor destroys man's natural desires; rather, it provides a most pure and normal environment for those natural desires, one free of any artificial provocation.

In this context, the basic principle of Islam's system of moral training is blocking the means. Islam closes the very doors that lead to straying, eliminates the causes that become means of leading man astray, or provide the causes of temptation, or through which emotions of man are inflamed. On the other hand, Islam also provides people with the means of natural gratification, within the bounds of the law.

Islam deeply respects the family and the sanctity of the home. Therefore, the first principle established is that no one may enter someone's home without the permission of its inhabitants. This is solely so that the eyes of the one entering do not see any scene that the household wishes to keep hidden. Now, if someone enters suddenly and the household is unprepared, they would not like that sight. Furthermore, Islam also commands that all men and women lower their gaze, and that women do not go out adorned with beautification.

Along with this, Islam provides opportunities for the poor and the needy to marry, because the best weapon against immorality is to bring all people within the secure fortress of marriage. Likewise, it is commanded that slave girls should not be compelled to immorality, since immorality can very easily be spread through slave girls.
