And say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts, and not display their adornment except what necessarily appears of it, and that they should draw their head-coverings over their chests, and not display their adornment except to their husbands, their fathers, their husbands' fathers, their sons, their husbands' sons, their brothers, their brothers' sons, their sisters' sons, their women, those whom their right hands possess, male attendants who have no physical desire, or children who are not yet aware of women's private matters. And they should not stamp their feet so as to reveal what they conceal of their adornment. O believers, turn to Allah in repentance, all of you, that perhaps you may prosper.﴾ (30:31)

The aim of these verses is to establish a very pure and clean society, one in which there is not constant sexual agitation everywhere and at all times, and in which there are not constant means of enjoying flesh and bone. Measures that continually stir up sexual excitement, and as a result produce a thirst that is never quenched, are harmful. A malicious glance, a seductive gesture, the display of adornment, and the exposure of the body can set the feelings of others on fire. They do not merely awaken the dormant animality within a person, but also create restlessness in the other party. The other side then loses control over itself. Either the person falls prey to unrestrained sexual indulgence, or nervous and psychological disorders arise within him, and in this way a person is afflicted with suffering.

Islam, which seeks to build a pure and clean society, adopts as its first measure for establishing it the protection of feelings from agitation. It preserves the natural inclinations found in both parties, and gives this natural impulse a protected and constructive form in accordance with its natural pattern.

There came a period in human history when the doctrine of ibahiyyah (permissiveness) spread. Free conversation between the sexes, free mixing, and idle chatter were made common, to the extent that children began to be given sexual education, and the most secret matters were brought into the open. These things and measures were undertaken under the doctrine that they protect people from the harms of suppressing sexual inclination and sexual feelings, and that they give people the opportunity to make sexual arrangements freely as they wish. These doctrines permitted this so that people would not commit violence and other wrongdoing in the sexual sphere.

This sexual freedom became prevalent when purely materialist views about human beings spread, and the human being was declared to be merely an animal, especially after the spread of Freud's sexual ideas. But I myself observed these doctrines in a country where there was complete permissiveness, and where none of the religious, moral or human restraints existed. Yet I observed that all these doctrines are mere assumptions, and that the conditions of such countries utterly refute them.

We have also seen countries in which there is no restriction on physical union, nudity, and sexual licentiousness. There, all its possible forms are lawful. But in those countries sexual relations did not become civilised, nor did any regularity arise within them. Rather, sexual thirst grew to the point of madness, and grew so much that the very trace of satisfaction disappeared. In those countries a flood of sexual and psychological diseases broke out, and problems emerged that arise from sexual deprivation. These problems are found abundantly in those societies in which there is no restriction on sexual anarchy. These problems arose simply because in such countries there was no sexual restraint or discipline. Sexual friendships were free without any obstacle, and sexual relations and unions were seen on the roads like those of cattle. Sexual movements and lustful glances were quite ordinary things. The detailed events and detailed conduct of these countries cannot be discussed here. For details, see Muhammad Qutb's book (Al-Insan bayna al-Maddiyyah wal-Islam), the chapter on sexual problems. For further details, see my forthcoming book (Amrika allati Ra'ayt) (America as I Saw It).

Attraction between men and women is a natural matter, and it has been innately placed within human beings, because the continuity of life on this earth depends upon it. Human beings have the responsibility of discharging the duties of vicegerency (khilafah) on the earth. A large and important part of this responsibility is to maintain the continuity of life here. Therefore this attraction is a permanent attraction. Sometimes it falls asleep and then awakens again. As soon as it awakens, it is fulfilled only when union between the two sexes takes place and satisfaction is achieved. If this physical satisfaction does not occur, its effect falls upon the human nerves, and in such circumstances a person feels intense oppression. Then even a glance can incite him, a gesture can incite him, and even a slight smile can arouse him. As a result of mere idle chatter, a person becomes uncontrollable, and even a beautiful voice can set him trembling. Therefore the safe course is to protect a person within society from such occasions, so that his sexual inclination remains within natural limits, and so that opportunities for his satisfaction are provided through lawful and natural means. Islam adopts precisely this method. Alongside this, Islam also turns a person's powers towards other constructive directions. The other affairs of life are of greater importance than the mere union of body, soul, flesh and bone, so sexual gratification does not remain the only goal before a person. The verses under discussion put into operation exactly such policies of Islam, namely: reducing the occasions that produce agitation, engaging people in lofty objectives, and then creating opportunities for lawful satisfaction for both parties.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 24, verse 30:

(Qul lil-mu'mineen... bima yasna'oon) (24:30) "". Lowering the gaze on the part of men is a psychological discipline and refinement, and the search for natural and physical beauty in other human beings, and the beauty of the face, is a natural impulse present in every person. In this way a believer keeps control over this impulse. Moreover, this is a step that closes the first door of deviation. If the gaze is not restrained, the human glance can plunge a person into temptation. It is, as it were, the first attempt to protect oneself from a poisoned arrow.

When a person gains control over his glances, his private parts will automatically come under control as a consequence. By lowering the gaze, a person is saved from entering the second stage of deviation. This is why lowering the gaze and guarding the private parts are brought together in one verse, because lowering the gaze is the cause and guarding the private parts is the effect. Indeed, in both the realm of conscience and the realm of action, these are the first and second steps, and they are close to one another.

"Dhalika azka lahum" (That is purer for them). This is a purer way for their emotions. By this method they will be saved from falling into evil, and their inclination will be confined to the lawful path. It is Allah who commands you to adopt these precautionary measures. This is natural and psychological education and training. Allah is aware of all your actions, and He is All-Knowing and All-Aware.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 24, verse 31:

(وقل۔۔۔۔۔۔ فروجھن) (24 : 31) "And say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze, and guard their private parts." They should not leave their hungry glances free, nor look at men with lustful eyes. They should not cast a sudden glance at them in a way that would stir up the dormant inclinations of men, and they should not make themselves lawful for men who are not lawful for them. They should use their natural inclinations in a lawful manner and bring forth legitimate children, and it should not happen that illegitimate children are born, who become a cause of shame for the society, and the society becomes a source of disgrace for them.

(ولا۔۔۔۔۔ منھا) (24 : 31) "And not to display their adornment except that which appears thereof." Adornment, beautification and makeup are permissible for women, because they are a demand of their nature. Every woman has the natural desire to appear very beautiful. The standards of adornment change in every age, but the impulse toward adornment exists within nature, and it is this: that a woman should make herself as beautiful as possible.

Islam does not uproot this nature of woman either. It accepts it, but Islam certainly organizes and regulates it. Islam wishes that this beauty and adornment be specific only to one man, namely her husband and life partner, and that only he should see this adornment. No one else should share in it. Yes, some mahrams may also share in this adornment, who are mentioned later, and from whom it is not expected that the woman would be sexually arousing to them.

As for the adornment that is on the face or that is on the hands, its display is permissible, because uncovering the face and hands is permissible for women. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Asma bint Abi Bakr: "Asma, when a woman reaches the age of menstruation, it is not permissible that any part be exposed except these," and he indicated towards the face and the hands.

Wal-yadribna bi-khumurihinna 'ala juyubihinna (24 : 31) "And let them draw their head-coverings over their bosoms." Juyub is the plural of jayb, which refers to the slit in a shirt at the chest. And khimar refers to the cloth that is worn over the head, so that by it the chest is covered, and it remains hidden from lustful glances, and these places are also protected from a sudden glance. The pious people do not prolong that sudden glance, nor do they look a second time, but even that glance sometimes gives rise to great trials, if those places connected with sexual inclination are left uncovered. Allah does not wish to test any human being in this matter, because Allah knows that for humans this is a great trial.

And those believing women who were abiding by the prohibition from Allah, and whose hearts were illuminated by the light of Allah, did not show the slightest hesitation in carrying out these commands, even though their natural inclination and desire was to display such beauty and grace as every woman naturally desires. In the age of ignorance, it was the custom, just as the custom of today's modern ignorance is, that women would walk among men with their chests thrown out, and nothing would be upon their chests. Sometimes their necks and locks of hair would also be exposed, and their earrings would also be visible. When the command came from Allah that they should let their head-coverings fall over their chests and display only those parts of their adornment that are apparent, they did not hesitate in the least in carrying out this command. Regarding this, the saying of Hazrat 'Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) explains it well: May Allah have mercy on the early emigrant women, when this verse was revealed:

Wal-yadribna bi-khumurihinna 'ala juyubihinna (24 : 31) "And let them draw their head-coverings over their bosoms." So when their men went to the women and recited this verse to them, a revolution came about. A man would recite it before his wife, his sister, his daughter, or other close female relatives, and those women tore their embroidered silk shawls and covered their heads with them. They did this out of the spirit of faith and affirmation (that is, they acted upon the command of Allah when it came). And those women could be seen standing in rows behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as if birds were sitting upon their heads.

Islam transformed the taste of Islamic society itself, and in that society the aesthetic sensibilities of people changed. Now the animal allures of beauty and attractiveness were no longer sought or admired, but a human and refined style, manner and standard of beauty was established, in which nakedness ceased to be the standard of beauty. As far as nakedness is concerned, it is the animal standard of beauty. A person is inclined towards it only when his sensibilities become animal. Even if this naked beauty presents a very high degree of attractiveness, the beauty of seriousness and dignity is that pure beauty which Islam presents. Through it taste develops, and it is worthy of man. It is outward and it is also imaginative.

Even today Islam trains truly believing women in this same manner, although today's environment has changed greatly. Generally the taste of people has fallen, and the animal hue predominates in it. In today's aesthetic manifestations, nakedness and animal styles are at their height, but our believing women still conceal their places of attraction and places of trial. They are struggling in this jihad in an environment where there is nothing but nakedness. The condition of women is that they are inviting men to look, and they are calling and summoning in the manner that an animal calls to another animal. This veiling and seriousness is the only measure for the protection of the Islamic individual and of a moderate Islamic society from immorality. But where there is no fear of trial, immorality and deviation, Islam does not prohibit uncovering and display of adornment. Thus, for those men whose inclination is generally not towards mahram women, there is no prohibition on displaying adornment before them.

The fathers, sons, fathers-in-law, sons of husbands, brothers, nephews, sisters' sons, and believing women are exempt from these commands.

Aw nisaihinna (24 : 31) "or their women," meaning believing women. As for non-believing women, they are not exempt. This is because it is possible that non-Muslim women may relate to their husbands, or brothers, or sons, the hidden adornments and stories of Muslim women. In the Sahihayn there is:

"No woman should be naked before another woman, so that she describes her to her husband as if he is looking at her." But Muslim women are exempt from this because they are trustworthy. Their religion and their sincerity do not permit them to describe the physical build and adornment of a Muslim woman before their husbands. And they are also exempt from this.

Aw ma malakat aymanuhunna (24 : 31) "or those whom your right hands possess." Regarding them there are two opinions. One is that it refers only to female slaves; the other is that both male and female slaves are included in this command, because a male slave generally does not look at his mistress with lustful glances. But the first opinion is correct, because a slave is nevertheless a human being, and upon seeing the places of adornment of his mistress, a sexual agitation may arise within him, even though he may hold a lower status socially. And those subordinate men who have no other purpose are also exempt, that is:

Awi-t-tabi'ina ghayri uli-l-irbati mina-r-rijal (24 : 31) "or the male attendants who have no physical desire." Or those who, for some reason, have no desire for women, such as those who are impotent, or foolish, or insane, or any other cause due to which they do not desire a woman, and there is no danger of trial or deviation.

Awi-t-tifli-lladhina lam yazharu 'ala 'awrati-n-nisa' (24 : 31) "or the children who are not yet aware of the private matters of women." Children who, if they see a woman naked, would not develop bodily desire within them. If sexual consciousness has arisen in them, even though they have not reached puberty, then a veil from them is necessary, and they do not fall within this exception.

All of these are other than husbands. For them it is permissible that they may see any part of a woman's body other than the area below the navel and above the knee, provided there is no fear from these people that they will fall into trial. As for the husband, he is permitted to see every part of his wife's body.

The purpose and intent of these commands of veiling was that no one should fall into deviation and immorality, therefore here the prohibition is also extended to such actions through which one may fall into trial, through which the arousal of desire may be stirred, and through which hidden emotions may be inflamed, even though practically those women are in purdah.

Wa la yadribna bi-arjulihinna li-yu'lama ma yukhfina min zinatihinna (24 : 31) "And let them not stamp their feet so that what they conceal of their adornment becomes known." This verse penetrates to the depths of the formation of the human self, its impression, its receptiveness, and its response in sexual matters. The truth is that human thought and imagination sometimes influence a person even more than seeing a scene. Many people are so sensitive that they are affected by seeing a woman's shoes, her clothes and her jewelry more than by seeing her body. Moreover, for some individuals the thought of a woman affects them more than her presence before them. Scholars of psychology have much knowledge about these matters. Likewise, the sound of anklets from afar and the fragrance of perfume also stir up the human senses and have effects on their nerves. Sometimes these effects are so intense that a person loses control over himself. The Holy Qur'an closes all these channels of influence, because the One who revealed the Qur'an is the One who created the human being. He is the One who knows His creation best. He is aware with the utmost depth.

And finally, the source of all good deeds comes, that people's connection with Allah should be strong, and the door of repentance and seeking forgiveness is also left open for them. That is, Allah will forgive those sins which you people committed before the revelation of the Qur'an.

(Wa tubu ilallahi jami'an ayyuhal-mu'minuna la'allakum tuflihun) (24 : 31) "O believers, all of you turn to Allah in repentance, that perhaps you may attain success." Thus through this phrase awareness of Allah's supervision is awakened, and the importance of Allah's greatness and His mercy is conveyed, because in this struggle against Satan, He alone is the helper, and fear of Him and awareness of His supervision alone can protect a person from these corruptions.

Up to this point the preventive remedy of this problem has been presented, but human sexual desire is in fact a real desire placed within humans. Therefore there is also a need for the true remedy of sexual fulfillment, that is, the positive remedy. This positive remedy would be that marriage be made easy in society, that assistance be provided in this matter, and that severity be applied to all other means and relationships in comparison with marriage and lawful union.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 24, verses 32–33:

(Marry off ... All-Encompassing, All-Knowing. And let those who ... Forgiving, Merciful.)

The best way to satisfy sexual desire is marriage. The secret of nature and of the Creator within this deep urge is that people should gladly carry out the difficult task of continuing the human race. Therefore we must remove every obstacle standing in the way of marriage, so that life continues simply and in accordance with its natural course. The first obstacle to the formation of a family is financial. In this way people cannot remain protected and fortified. Since Islam is a complete system of life, it makes chastity and purity obligatory only when it also provides the means for them, and provides them to all members of society. Thus, those who deviate from the moderate and natural path are not compelled to do so, but find the correct path to sexual fulfilment before them. This is why Islam commands that a path to marriage be made easy for young people who are unmarried.

﴿Marry off those among you who are single, and the righteous among your male and female slaves. If they are poor, Allah will enrich them out of His bounty; Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ (24:32) Those who are single (ayama) are people who have no mate: a woman without a husband, or a man without a wife. Here the intended meaning is those who are free. After this, slaves are specifically mentioned.

﴿And the righteous among your male and female slaves﴾ (24:32). But these people often have poor financial circumstances.

﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them out of His bounty﴾ (24:32). This command is for Islamic society: that it should arrange marriage. The majority of scholars (jumhur al-ulama) hold that this is a recommended matter (mustahabb). This is because in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ there were unmarried people who had not married. If this command were obligatory (fard), the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would certainly have arranged their marriages.

In my view, this command is obligatory (wajib), not in the sense that an unmarried person should be compelled to marry, but in the sense that it is obligatory upon Islamic society to assist those who wish to marry, so that they may be protected within the fortress of marriage. This is the practical safeguard against falling into obscenity and adultery, and only in this way can society be protected from immorality. If protecting society from immorality is an obligation, then taking the necessary measures for this obligation is also an obligation.

From this it also becomes clear that since Islam is a complete and coherent system of life, it establishes an economic system in which every person has equal opportunities for economic struggle, so that no one has to depend on the public treasury (Bayt al-Mal) for their needs. In some exceptional circumstances, the public treasury should also be ready to provide assistance. The fundamental principle of the Islamic economic system is that every person eats from their own earnings. The duty placed upon society is to provide opportunities for work for all. As for people being given assistance from the public treasury, this happens only in exceptional cases.

If people strive and live according to the Islamic system, and yet circumstances arise in which, purely because of economic necessity, there are unmarried young men and women in the Islamic society, then it is an obligation upon Islamic society and the Islamic government to give financial assistance to such people. The same ruling applies to male and female slaves: it is the duty of their owners to arrange their marriages, if they are able to do so.

It is also the duty of Islamic society to see that if people, whether men or women, wish to marry but poverty stands as an obstacle in their way, then society should remove those obstacles, because provision is in the hand of Allah. Allah can make them independent, provided they adopt the lawful way (halal).

﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them out of His bounty﴾ (24:32). The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Three types of people have a right upon Allah that He should help them: the fighter in the way of Allah, the slave who makes a written agreement to pay for his freedom, and the one who marries in order to protect himself from unlawful paths." (Tirmidhi and Nasa'i)

As long as the circumstances of the unmarried are not corrected, and Islamic society does not make arrangements for them, Allah commands them to hold fast to chastity and purity.

﴿And let those who cannot find a means to marry keep chaste until Allah enriches them from His bounty﴾ (24:33). Allah does not place hardship on any person, for Allah possesses all-encompassing knowledge.

"Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing" (wallahu wasi'un alim). In this way Islam finds a most practical solution to this problem. Every person who is able to marry is commanded to marry, even if they are weak in financial terms, because the one who resolves financial matters is Allah.

In that period, the institution of slavery existed in the Islamic system out of necessity, and because moral values are weaker among slaves, the slaves present within Islamic society were becoming an obstacle to establishing high moral standards in society. Islam initially kept the institution of slavery in place because slaves existed among the disbelievers, and any Muslims who fell into their hands were also made slaves. Keeping the present situation in view, Islam sought to resolve the sexual problem by arranging the marriages of slaves. To end slavery itself through its own means, Islam devised the method of mukatabah (a written contract for manumission), such that if a slave offers to pay financial compensation, the owner is bound to accept it.

﴿And those of your slaves who seek a written agreement (of manumission), write it for them if you know good in them﴾ (24:33). Scholars differ in their opinions as to whether this is obligatory or not; that is, whether, if the slave makes the offer, the mukatabah is binding or is at the discretion of the owner. I hold that it is obligatory, because the view of obligation is the one that agrees with Islam's overall policy. Islam regards the human being as an honoured creature, and the existence of slavery is contrary to human dignity. After the agreement, whatever the slave earns will belong to the owner, so that the compensation of the agreed sum can be paid. Likewise, it becomes necessary to assist such a slave from the funds of zakat, so that the slave may attain freedom as quickly as possible.

﴿And give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you﴾ (24:33), on the condition that the owner judges that there is good in the slave. The first good is Islam. After that, good means that the slave has the ability to earn a living. It should not be that after gaining freedom he goes around begging from people. Sometimes such a person may adopt morally degraded means of livelihood, through which he can earn only enough to sustain his life. Since Islam is a complete and harmonious system, it also takes into account the real situation. Its purpose is not merely that it should become known that a slave has been freed; mere title and name have no importance in Islam. Islam looks at reality, to see whether this freed slave will actually be able, after his freedom, to play a constructive role in society. This is possible only when the person is able to earn something, does not become a burden on people, and does not adopt filthy means of livelihood. If he begins to sell things that are more precious than freedom (for example, prostitution), while he is being freed so that society may be purified and not so that society may be corrupted through him, and his act becomes a more severe calamity for society. (In the modern age, because slavery has ended through international agreements, in practice there will now be no slavery in Islam either.)

In Islamic society, a more dangerous disease than slavery is considered to be the use of slaves for prostitution. Among the people of Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance) it was customary that whoever owned a slave girl would let her practise this profession and would impose a tax on her, and this profession has continued in the world to this day. Since Islam commanded that Islamic society be purified of every kind of fornication (zina), the Qur'an specifically mentioned this kind of zina.

﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution, when they desire chastity, in order to seek the transitory gain of worldly life. And whoever compels them, then indeed Allah is, after their compulsion, Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (24:33). Through this verse, those who used to compel their slave girls into this profession were forbidden, and they were warned not to accumulate worldly wealth through such wicked means. To those slave girls who had been compelled in this way, a promise was given that their sins would be forgiven, because in such a case they were compelled. Sa'di says that this verse was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul. He was the leader of the hypocrites (munafiqin). He had a slave girl named Mu'adhah. His practice was that whenever a guest came to him, he would send this slave girl to him, for two purposes: one, that the man might give some reward, and the other, that in this way he would show hospitality to the guest. This slave girl came to Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) and complained about this matter. Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) took the slave girl into his own possession. Upon this, Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul called out to his people, asking who would rescue them from Muhammad ﷺ, since he had now begun laying hands on their property. Then this verse was revealed.

This measure, that slave girls should not be used for fornication, is one of the measures of the Islamic system through which the Islamic society was purified of fornication, and all unnatural and filthy paths of sexual gratification were closed. This is because if the profession of prostitution exists, many people may fall into it because of its availability. If it does not exist, people will again wish to marry and live a pure life.

Some people say that the existence of this profession is a guarantee of peace and security in the homes of respectable people, because if marriage becomes difficult, then a person can fulfil his natural need through that filthy path. If this path is not kept lawful, then wolves will begin to play with the honour of respectable people.

Those who think along this line are in fact reversing the relationship between cause and effect. What should happen is that people's sexual inclinations be kept pure and be organised in such a way that they become a means for the continuation of the line of human life. This duty every society must fulfil: it must establish an economic system through which every person is capable of being bound in the bond of marriage. If even then some find difficulties in marriage, such cases can be given special treatment. In this way no one will be compelled into this filthy profession, and the situation will not be that filth is found everywhere, the street is a heap of filth, and whoever passes along it throws filth there while society watches.

Only the economic system of a country can eliminate such filth, in such a way that such filth is not gathered in any place. There should not be a situation where, purely for economic reasons, justification is provided for this filth. Heaps of filth should not be made available for human beings.

This is the policy that Islam uses for the purification of society. Because of it, a great revolution takes place in any society: the heavens are transformed on earth, and the gaze of all people is set on high horizons for lofty purposes. They see by the light of Allah, and by it their horizons are illuminated.

As long as the circumstances of the unmarried are not corrected, and Islamic society does not make arrangements for them, Allah commands them to hold fast to chastity and purity.

﴿And let those who cannot find a means to marry keep chaste until Allah enriches them from His bounty﴾ (24:33). Allah does not place hardship on any person, for Allah possesses all-encompassing knowledge.

"Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing" (wallahu wasi'un alim). In this way Islam finds a most practical solution to this problem. Every person who is able to marry is commanded to marry, even if they are weak in financial terms, because the one who resolves financial matters is Allah.

In that period, the institution of slavery existed in the Islamic system out of necessity, and because moral values are weaker among slaves, the slaves present within Islamic society were becoming an obstacle to establishing high moral standards in society. Islam initially kept the institution of slavery in place because slaves existed among the disbelievers, and any Muslims who fell into their hands were also made slaves. Keeping the present situation in view, Islam sought to resolve the sexual problem by arranging the marriages of slaves. To end slavery itself through its own means, Islam devised the method of mukatabah (a written contract for manumission), such that if a slave offers to pay financial compensation, the owner is bound to accept it.

﴿And those of your slaves who seek a written agreement (of manumission), write it for them if you know good in them﴾ (24:33). Scholars differ in their opinions as to whether this is obligatory or not; that is, whether, if the slave makes the offer, the mukatabah is binding or is at the discretion of the owner. I hold that it is obligatory, because the view of obligation is the one that agrees with Islam's overall policy. Islam regards the human being as an honoured creature, and the existence of slavery is contrary to human dignity. After the agreement, whatever the slave earns will belong to the owner, so that the compensation of the agreed sum can be paid. Likewise, it becomes necessary to assist such a slave from the funds of zakat, so that the slave may attain freedom as quickly as possible.

﴿And give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you﴾ (24:33), on the condition that the owner judges that there is good in the slave. The first good is Islam. After that, good means that the slave has the ability to earn a living. It should not be that after gaining freedom he goes around begging from people. Sometimes such a person may adopt morally degraded means of livelihood, through which he can earn only enough to sustain his life. Since Islam is a complete and harmonious system, it also takes into account the real situation. Its purpose is not merely that it should become known that a slave has been freed; mere title and name have no importance in Islam. Islam looks at reality, to see whether this freed slave will actually be able, after his freedom, to play a constructive role in society. This is possible only when the person is able to earn something, does not become a burden on people, and does not adopt filthy means of livelihood. If he begins to sell things that are more precious than freedom (for example, prostitution), while he is being freed so that society may be purified and not so that society may be corrupted through him, and his act becomes a more severe calamity for society. (In the modern age, because slavery has ended through international agreements, in practice there will now be no slavery in Islam either.)

In Islamic society, a more dangerous disease than slavery is considered to be the use of slaves for prostitution. Among the people of Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance) it was customary that whoever owned a slave girl would let her practise this profession and would impose a tax on her, and this profession has continued in the world to this day. Since Islam commanded that Islamic society be purified of every kind of fornication (zina), the Qur'an specifically mentioned this kind of zina.

﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution, when they desire chastity, in order to seek the transitory gain of worldly life. And whoever compels them, then indeed Allah is, after their compulsion, Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (24:33). Through this verse, those who used to compel their slave girls into this profession were forbidden, and they were warned not to accumulate worldly wealth through such wicked means. To those slave girls who had been compelled in this way, a promise was given that their sins would be forgiven, because in such a case they were compelled. Sa'di says that this verse was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul. He was the leader of the hypocrites (munafiqin). He had a slave girl named Mu'adhah. His practice was that whenever a guest came to him, he would send this slave girl to him, for two purposes: one, that the man might give some reward, and the other, that in this way he would show hospitality to the guest. This slave girl came to Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) and complained about this matter. Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) took the slave girl into his own possession. Upon this, Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul called out to his people, asking who would rescue them from Muhammad ﷺ, since he had now begun laying hands on their property. Then this verse was revealed.

This measure, that slave girls should not be used for fornication, is one of the measures of the Islamic system through which the Islamic society was purified of fornication, and all unnatural and filthy paths of sexual gratification were closed. This is because if the profession of prostitution exists, many people may fall into it because of its availability. If it does not exist, people will again wish to marry and live a pure life.

Some people say that the existence of this profession is a guarantee of peace and security in the homes of respectable people, because if marriage becomes difficult, then a person can fulfil his natural need through that filthy path. If this path is not kept lawful, then wolves will begin to play with the honour of respectable people.

Those who think along this line are in fact reversing the relationship between cause and effect. What should happen is that people's sexual inclinations be kept pure and be organised in such a way that they become a means for the continuation of the line of human life. This duty every society must fulfil: it must establish an economic system through which every person is capable of being bound in the bond of marriage. If even then some find difficulties in marriage, such cases can be given special treatment. In this way no one will be compelled into this filthy profession, and the situation will not be that filth is found everywhere, the street is a heap of filth, and whoever passes along it throws filth there while society watches.

Only the economic system of a country can eliminate such filth, in such a way that such filth is not gathered in any place. There should not be a situation where, purely for economic reasons, justification is provided for this filth. Heaps of filth should not be made available for human beings.

This is the policy that Islam uses for the purification of society. Because of it, a great revolution takes place in any society: the heavens are transformed on earth, and the gaze of all people is set on high horizons for lofty purposes. They see by the light of Allah, and by it their horizons are illuminated.

This is the final commentary on this lesson, which fits well with its theme.

(And We have certainly sent down to you clear verses...) (34)

These verses explain the matter clearly. There is no complexity or difficulty in them that would prevent them from being understood, nor is the firm system of life they prescribe beyond anyone's comprehension. This system is such that the experiences of past nations also bear witness to its soundness, and the Qur'an has related the histories of such nations. Moreover, every human being in the world desires that a high-minded, advanced and pure society be established, one founded upon the fear of God. Islam is precisely such a system of life.

The decisions and commands that have come down throughout this entire lesson are in harmony with this introduction and commentary, the purpose of which is to create in the hearts of people the fear of God and a bond with God.

Lesson No. 154: An Overview

In the two preceding lessons of this surah, the remedy was given for those material desires of man that are natural to human personality and that hold a deep grip over it. The aim was to purify these desires and to raise them to the luminous horizon. The lusts of flesh and skin, the desires of the eyes and the private parts. The explanation and criticism of these matters. The problems of anger, provocation and enmity arising in this context were resolved, and guidance was given.

It was ordered that in the Islamic society the spread of obscenity be avoided. Prohibition of obscenity was enforced in practical life and in human speech. In the matter of preventing these things, severe strictness was also applied in punishments. Strict laws were made for the hadd of zina and the hadd of qadhf. Then, through the example of the accusation and slander against chaste and innocent married women, a lesson was given. Preventive laws were made for these matters and moral instructions were also given. The rules of lowering the gaze and seeking permission were enforced. Everything that could lead to falling into temptation or could stir up lust was forbidden. Then the encouragement to marry, the prohibition of prostitution, and the encouragement to free slaves: all these matters are related to the aim that the agitations of flesh and blood be restrained, and that in people there be produced the consciousness of purity, self-control, and the drive toward cleanliness, luminosity and spirituality.

After the incident of the ifk, the traces of rage, enmity and bitterness that remained in society were all sought to be healed, and the anguish and restlessness that had arisen in the souls of the believers, and because of which the lofty human standards had been shaken, were treated. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was fully reassured and his restlessness was removed. Hadrat Aisha (رضي الله عنها) not only became content and satisfied but also became happy. Hadrat Abu Bakr (رضي الله عنه) also became satisfied and calm. Safwan ibn Mu'attal emerged from under a great burden. The doubts of all the people of Islam were removed, and those who had spoken wrongly in that incident returned and repented. The doubts of all people were removed, and the rain of Allah's grace, guidance and mercy fell upon all. Through this teaching and refinement, and through this guidance and direction, the human soul was purified and cleansed and made luminous. Now its gaze turned toward the lofty horizon in the direction of this new light, and throughout the heavens and the earth the believers began to see the light of their Lord. Allah granted the people of Islam the capacity to take from the horizons of the universe this luminosity.

Lesson No. 154: Explanation of the Verses

35 to 45

(Allahu nurus-samawati wal-ard ... nurun ala nur) "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. His light is like a niche in which is a lamp, the lamp is within a glass, the glass is like a glittering star, and it is lit from the oil of a blessed olive tree that is neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it. Light upon light."

This is an example that brings the conception of an unlimited greatness close to limited human perception, and a very small image of light is presented that the human imagination can grasp, because the true light of Allah cannot be comprehended by human conception. A small example of light is presented, while human perception cannot encompass the horizons of that light which lie beyond its limits.

From this vast cosmos we now come to a niche, which is in a wall, where a lamp is placed, so that its light illuminates the whole room. The lamp is in the niche, the lamp is in a glass; this glass protects the lamp from the wind, so its light becomes clear and its luminosity increases. This glass is such that it is like a shining star. The glass itself is also like clear, transparent and bright crystal. Here a link is established between the example and the reality, and the difference between the original and the model becomes known. The imagination is led from a small glass to a great star, so that human thought does not remain confined to that small model. The example of the small lamp is adopted only as an indication toward this reality; after pointing to the shining star, the discourse now returns to explain that same small example.

Yuqadu min shajaratin mubarakatin zaytunatin (24:35) "It is kindled from a blessed tree, an olive." Up to that time, the light of olive oil was the cleanest and brightest of all lights. But this example is not given merely because the light of olive oil is the purest. Rather, the intended indication is the sanctity that the olive tree possesses, that this tree grows in the sacred valley of Tuwa. The olives that came to the Arabs came from the sacred valley of Sinai. The Quran refers to this tree.

Wa shajaratan takhruju min Tur Sayna tanbutu bid-duhni wa sibghin lil-akilin: "And a tree that grows out of Mount Sinai, which produces oil and a relish for those who eat." This is a tree of very long life, and all its parts are useful to human beings. Its oil, its wood, its leaves and its fruit are all beneficial. Now the discourse rises a little above this small example and turns the mind toward the original. This is not a particular tree. "It is neither of the east nor of the west." Nor is it a limited and specific oil. It is an oil of its own kind, of another nature.

Yakadu zaytuha yudi'u wa law lam tamsashu nar: "Its oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it." That is, light is overflowing within it. Light upon light. By the words nurun ala nur our attention is directed toward the supreme luminosity of the Divine Being.

This is the divine light by which the darkness of this whole universe is dispelled. This is the light whose reality the human mind cannot reach. It is only an effort that hearts be attached to it, strive for its perception, and hope to see it.

(Yahdi Allahu li-nurihi man yasha'...) (35)

Allah guides to His light whomever He wills, but only the one who opens his heart and mind to accept that light. This light is spread throughout the heavens and the earth. Its bounties and blessings are present in the heavens and the earth and remain present at all times. This light never ends, never dims and never switches off. Whenever a person turns toward it, he sees it, and whenever a wayward person turns toward it, it guides him. And whenever anyone establishes a connection with this light, it gives him guidance.

The example given in this verse of Allah's light is for the purpose of making people understand. "He makes the example for people." This is because He is the All-Knowing and knows well the limits of human perceptive capacity. The light explained in these examples is absolute light, common throughout the heavens and the earth. Its overflow is upon the heavens and the earth, and this light is seen shining and glowing in those houses in which people's hearts are attached to Allah, in which the remembrance of Allah continues, who fear Allah, whose inhabitants are people of Allah, and in whose hearts this light of the heavens is preferred over everything in the world.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 24, verses 36–39:

(Fi buyutin… wal-asal, rijal… wal-absar, liyajziyahumullahu… bi-ghayri hisab) (36 to 83)

Here there is a particular connection between the parable of Allah's light and the parable of these houses, and this is a great feature of the Qur'an's manner of expression. The lamp burning inside the niche and the believing heart shining inside the houses: thus there is a correspondence (mushakalah) between the two.

These houses are such that Allah has commanded that their walls be raised and that they be built. To "raise" them by the permission (idhn) is to command that they be built, so that people act upon that command. Accordingly, these houses have been established, they are lofty, and they are pure and clean. Their scene resembles the scene of this universe, in which the light of the Lord is spread out. The loftiness of these houses is so that the name of Allah may be mentioned in them.

"Yudhkaru fihasmuh" (24:36): "In them His name is remembered." And these pure hearts are attached to Allah, they glorify Allah, they fear Allah, they perform prayer, and they give in the way of Allah.

"Rijalun la tulhihim… wa itaa'iz-zakah" (24:37): "Men whom neither trade nor commerce distracts from the remembrance of Allah, from the establishment of prayer, and from paying zakah; they glorify Him morning and evening." Trade and commerce are means of earning and accumulating wealth. These are people who, despite being occupied with these affairs, are not heedless of the rights of Allah, namely prayer, and of the rights of His servants, namely the payment of zakah.

"Yakhafuna yawman tataqallabu fihi al-qulubu wal-absar" (24:37): "They fear a Day in which hearts and eyes will be overturned." Hearts will be overturned, meaning there will be no stability within them due to fear and dread; and since these hearts fear Allah, trade and commerce cannot prevent them from the remembrance of Allah.

But hope is also attached to this fear. They do not despair. They keep their hopes bound to Allah.

"Liyajziyahumullahu ahsana ma 'amilu wa yazidahum min fadlih" (24:38): "So that Allah may reward them for the best of what they did and increase them from His bounty." Their hope is not frustrated either, because "Wallahu yarzuqu man yasha'u bi-ghayri hisab" (24:38): "Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning," since the bounty of Allah has no limits or bounds.

In contrast with that light which shines in the heavens and the earth, the light found in these houses of Allah, and the light shining in the hearts of the believers, the Qur'an here also presents a world of darkness and gloom. In that world there is no light, no peace or tranquility; fears cast their shadows everywhere, and destruction is everywhere. There is no good in it. This is the world of the disbelievers and the world of the unbeliever. Its features and manner are as follows.

"Wallatheena kafaru a'maluhum ka-sarabin biqi'atin yahsabuhu al-zam'anu ma'an… wa man lam yaj'al Allahu lahu nuran fama lahu min nur" (24:39–40): "As for those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a barren desert, which the thirsty one takes to be water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing, and there he finds Allah, who pays him his account in full, and Allah is swift in reckoning. Or they are like darkness in a deep sea, covered by a wave, above which is another wave, above which are clouds: darkness upon darkness. If a man stretches out his hand, he can barely see it. And he for whom Allah has not made a light, for him there is no light."

Here the Qur'an depicts the life of the disbelievers, their ideas and activities, in two ways. These are two scenes given as parables.

The first parable is of their deeds. These deeds appear as a mirage appears in a vast barren desert. The mirage looks like water. The thirsty one chases after it. He expects that on reaching the mirage he will drink water, but he is heedless of what he will actually find upon arrival. Here the scene changes suddenly. This person, who is running after the mirage, is thirsty and searching for water, and he is heedless of the matter that is about to befall him. When he reaches his destination, he finds no water. He finds there something he had never even thought of. Now, confronted with this new reality, he becomes terrified, and his hopes are cut off.

"Wa wajada Allaha 'indahu" (24:39): "There he finds Allah present." The Allah whom he denied is present, and this person was an enemy of Allah alone. In that mirage, Allah was awaiting him. If in that mirage this person were to find some worldly enemy, he would be terrified, but there he finds the Creator of the universe, who is the Compeller (Jabbar), of great power, and also severe in retribution. He is very swift in reckoning. Instead of water, there begins his reckoning and accounting there.

"Fawaffahu hisabahu wallahu sari'u al-hisab" (24:39): "Who paid him his account in full, and Allah is swift in reckoning." This scene presents, with speed and suddenness, a surprise; and the swift settling of accounts together with the mirage, and being suddenly struck with fear, form an artistic harmony.

The second scene is that after a false light, darkness descends, such that a person is in a ship, this ship is surrounded by the cruel waves of the sea, a wave rises above a wave, and black clouds have spread over them. Such a terrifying darkness has come that if a person wants to see his own hand he cannot see it, because of the intensity of fear and the intensity of darkness.

Disbelief is, in reality, a dense darkness within the waves of life. This darkness hides the light of Allah from sight. It is such a deep misguidance that in it a person cannot see even the proofs as near as his own hand. Disbelief is the name of a situation so frightening that in it a person has no peace or rest.

"Wa man lam yaj'al Allahu lahu nuran fama lahu min nur" (24:40): "He for whom Allah has not made a light, for him there is no light." What is the light of Allah? The guidance that Allah places in the heart of the believer is the light of Allah. This guidance opens up the human heart, and the human nature is renewed and harmonizes with the power of creation. Thus the light of Allah present in the human heart is united with the light of Allah present in this universe. And the person whose connection with this cosmic light has not been established remains in darkness, and nothing will appear to him. This will always be in frightening conditions in which there is no security. This person will fall into a misguidance from which escape is difficult, and the end of his deeds will be a mirage, and one who chases a mirage will obviously be destroyed. Because behind the deeds of the disbelievers there is no principle and no light. No deed is accepted without the light of faith, so no reformative work can be done without faith. The guidance of Allah is light, and the fear of Allah is light.

These were the scenes of disbelief and misguidance, and the scenes of darkness. After this, the scenes of faith and light come again in this universe. Here, throughout the whole universe, there is a state of light alone. All existences are glorifying in that light and are in a state of prayer: humans, jinn, the earth or the heavens, the living or the inanimate; the entire creation is glorifying, and all existences are companions in this sphere, such that the intuition of a wise person is stirred by it and the heart is filled with recognition.

Here there is a particular connection between the parable of Allah's light and the parable of these houses, and this is a great feature of the Qur'an's manner of expression. The lamp burning inside the niche and the believing heart shining inside the houses: thus there is a correspondence (mushakalah) between the two.

These houses are such that Allah has commanded that their walls be raised and that they be built. To "raise" them by the permission (idhn) is to command that they be built, so that people act upon that command. Accordingly, these houses have been established, they are lofty, and they are pure and clean. Their scene resembles the scene of this universe, in which the light of the Lord is spread out. The loftiness of these houses is so that the name of Allah may be mentioned in them.

"Yudhkaru fihasmuh" (24:36): "In them His name is remembered." And these pure hearts are attached to Allah, they glorify Allah, they fear Allah, they perform prayer, and they give in the way of Allah.

"Rijalun la tulhihim… wa itaa'iz-zakah" (24:37): "Men whom neither trade nor commerce distracts from the remembrance of Allah, from the establishment of prayer, and from paying zakah; they glorify Him morning and evening." Trade and commerce are means of earning and accumulating wealth. These are people who, despite being occupied with these affairs, are not heedless of the rights of Allah, namely prayer, and of the rights of His servants, namely the payment of zakah.

"Yakhafuna yawman tataqallabu fihi al-qulubu wal-absar" (24:37): "They fear a Day in which hearts and eyes will be overturned." Hearts will be overturned, meaning there will be no stability within them due to fear and dread; and since these hearts fear Allah, trade and commerce cannot prevent them from the remembrance of Allah.

But hope is also attached to this fear. They do not despair. They keep their hopes bound to Allah.

"Liyajziyahumullahu ahsana ma 'amilu wa yazidahum min fadlih" (24:38): "So that Allah may reward them for the best of what they did and increase them from His bounty." Their hope is not frustrated either, because "Wallahu yarzuqu man yasha'u bi-ghayri hisab" (24:38): "Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning," since the bounty of Allah has no limits or bounds.

In contrast with that light which shines in the heavens and the earth, the light found in these houses of Allah, and the light shining in the hearts of the believers, the Qur'an here also presents a world of darkness and gloom. In that world there is no light, no peace or tranquility; fears cast their shadows everywhere, and destruction is everywhere. There is no good in it. This is the world of the disbelievers and the world of the unbeliever. Its features and manner are as follows.

This person, who is running after the mirage, is thirsty and searching for water, and he is heedless of the matter that is about to befall him. When he reaches his destination, he finds no water. Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah al-Nur (24), verses 41–43:

(Alam tara ... yaf'aluna) (41) Man is not alone in this vast universe. He has an environment in which he lives, and it is a very vast environment. On his right and left, in every direction, the worship of Allah is taking place. In front of him, behind him, above him and below him, wherever the eye can reach, and beyond the limits of sight, wherever thought can reach, in this vast universe man has kindred beings. They have various forms and various natures, yet in one matter they are all alike: they are all creatures of Allah, all obedient to His command, and all busy in praising and glorifying Him.

Wa-Allahu 'alimun bima yaf'aluna (24:41) — "And Allah is aware of what they do." It is the distinctive method of the Qur'an's argumentation that it directs man's attention to his environment. In man's environment, in these heavens which are Allah's creation, all of it praises Allah. Man should reflect on the sight of this universe, because man sees his environment every day, and due to long familiarity his heart and mind are not affected by it. Look: some birds fly in this air, and their flight is in the form of rows. In this ordered and disciplined flight they are in fact declaring the praise of Allah and offering prayer.

Kullun qad 'alima salatahu wa tasbihahu (24:41) — "Each one knows its own prayer and its manner of glorification." Yet man, despite having such intellect and insight, is heedless of the glorification of Allah, although he is more than all other creatures obliged to be constantly engaged in glorification and prayer.

In this scene the whole universe appears prostrating with great humility before its Creator, standing in glorification and prayer. It is the natural state of the universe that it does so and that it follows the laws of nature ordained by Allah. When the human intuition becomes clear and pure, and as one hears the birds chirping morning and evening, one can clearly see that this whole universe is a singer of praise, and man can hear with his own ears the voice and glorification of this universe. If man attains recognition of his Lord, he then becomes in harmony and tune with the whole universe in this assembly of prayer and glorification, and sings along with it. When the Holy Prophet (ﷺ) heard the glorification of the pebbles beneath his feet, and when Prophet Dawud (David) recited the Psalms, this whole universe sang spiritual songs with them. They listened, and the beasts and birds all sang along with them.
